title: ii. dreams in the key of godhead — ron takes notes

nodes.text: ii. dreams in the key of godhead — ron takes notes
Ron catches me on the stairs after supper and asks if I have an hour. He asks it like he already knows the answer.

His room is the way Betty said it would be. Books on the floor in drifts, dust hanging in the lamplight, nowhere for a body to stand. He clears a place on the bed for me with his forearm. He sits at the desk half turned away.
The typewriter is black and the size of an engine block, and he rolls a fresh sheet into it and squares it and waits.
The page is blank except for a title typed at the top, centered, and underlined twice.
The springs give under me and books slide off the far edge of the bed one after another, like men stepping off a curb.
Where were you, the day before Jack found you on his floor?
I tell him Houston. I tell him a hospital. He doesn't ask what Houston is like now, or what a hospital is like. He asks something else.
What did the air smell like?
Cold. Rubbing alcohol. And something under the alcohol.
He types. The keys go off like rifle fire down a canyon, a burst, a pause, a burst. The bell rings at the end of the line and he throws the carriage back without looking at it.
And the light?
There were screens over every bed. A green line on each one, going up and down. Little lights all over the machines, blinking. Like eyes.
How many machines?
A whole floor of them. The whole top floor.
Did they fly?
I laugh, the first time in I don't know how long, and it hurts like a cough.
The helicopters did. They landed on the roof all night. Bringing people in.
He types a long time on that.
What color were their lights, coming down?
Red and white. When they're both going and it's hazy out, it comes through the blinds pink.
And the ones they carried in, were they awake?
Mostly not.
Who was in the room with him?
I tell him. My mother by the window. My sister, who had to leave for a shot so she could go to Brazil and study rocks the way he did. Me.
And where were you?

I tell him the floor. I tell him I slept next to the air conditioner because I did that when I was a kid, the hum of it. I tell him I slept through the worst part and woke up when it was already almost over. I haven't said that out loud to anybody.
I didn't know it was in me until it was out and in the room with the dust.
Ron doesn't stop typing to look at me. I am grateful to him for that.
Did they have to hold him down?
He tried to get up out of the bed. The drugs had him confused. They strapped him down and he fought them.
Did he say anything?
Not words, by then. He was angry. He sounded like he was begging for something.
Begging for what?
To go home. I think he wanted to go home.
He types, and I lean and watch the line come up out of the machine over his shoulder, letter by letter, black and wet.
A voice came booming from a machine among machines, it spoke a language not quite English, almost understandable. It was angry, desperate, pleading.
What did your father do?
Geologist. He taught. He took kids out into the field and showed them how to read a road cut. Oil, for a while.
Did he make you study?
He handed me books. Science fiction, mostly. Old paperbacks with the covers falling off.
Were they any good?
No. I read every one of them.
He types that too, or something like it. The bell rings.
And outside the hospital that night, what was the world doing?
Nothing. That's the thing. Cars on the freeway. Planes coming in to land. Everybody going to work in the morning. The world ended on one floor and nobody else got the memo.
He finds the line he wants and I watch it go down on the paper: the end of the world just outside, perhaps going on business as usual.
Do you mind?
I tell him no. I tell him take it. Somebody ought to.
How does it end?
He dies, Ron.
And the boy?

I lie back on his bed among the books. The typewriter goes on, burst and pause and bell, steady as a machine breathing for somebody. Down the hall Betty is laughing at something Jack said. The window is open and the air comes in heavy with oranges.
Ron asks me one more question. I am most of the way asleep by then and I don't catch what it is, only the shape of it, the way it lifts at the end.
